influences/christmas-customs/name: Christmas customs: Yule, trees, gifts and Saint Nicholas
influences/christmas-customs/sourceCultu: Roman Saturnalia and Kalends of January (feasting, gifts, greenery, lamps), and Germanic and Norse midwinter Yule (jól)
influences/christmas-customs/christianFo: The Twelve Days of Christmas with feasting, evergreens, the Christmas tree, gift-giving and Saint Nicholas / Father Christmas / Santa Claus
influences/christmas-customs/evidenceNot: Some Christmas customs clearly have pre-Christian Roman or Germanic forms. Midwinter feasting, decorating doors with greenery and lamps, New Year gifts (strenae) and the Scandinavian name jul are examples. Church leaders condemned these from the fourth century onwards, so we know they continued. Others are much later Christian or secular inventions with no proven pagan pedigree. These include the Christmas tree (sixteenth-century Alsace), the Yule log (seventeenth-century record), kissing under the mistletoe (eighteenth century) and Santa Claus (nineteenth-century New York). Each custom has to be judged separately.
influences/christmas-customs/popularClai: Every Christmas tradition, from the tree to Santa Claus, comes directly from pagan Yule or the Saturnalia, and the church simply put a Christian label on them.
influences/christmas-customs/whatHistori: Ronald Hutton, Bruce Forbes and Stephen Nissenbaum present Christmas as a layered festival. Late-antique Christians kept Roman New Year and midwinter customs, which preachers repeatedly denounced. Gregory of Nazianzus, in his Christmas oration of 380, told his flock not to garland their doors or hold dances. Asterius of Amasea and Caesarius of Arles attacked Kalends revelry, and the Council of Tours (567) declared the days from Christmas to Epiphany festal. In Scandinavia, Haakon the Good is said to have ordered Yule to be kept at Christmas in the tenth century (Snorri Sturluson, Heimskringla), and the name jul survived. But the decorated tree is first recorded in sixteenth-century Alsace and Germany, probably growing out of the 'paradise tree' of Adam-and-Eve plays on 24 December. Santa Claus developed from the cult of the fourth-century bishop Nicholas of Myra, Dutch Sinterklaas, Washington Irving (1809), 'A Visit from St Nicholas' (1823) and Thomas Nast's cartoons. The romantic idea that all of these are ancient pagan survivals owes much to nineteenth-century folklorists such as Jacob Grimm and James Frazer.
influences/christmas-customs/summary: Christmas absorbed some Roman midwinter and New Year customs and, in the north, the name and feasting of Yule. Many of its best-known features are medieval or modern, including the tree, the Yule log and Santa Claus. Historians judge each custom separately rather than calling them all 'pagan'.
influences/christmas-customs/story:
When the feast of Christ's birth spread in the fourth century, it landed in a season already full of celebration. The Saturnalia (17–23 December) featured feasting, gambling, role reversal and small gifts such as wax candles (cerei) and figurines (sigillaria). The Kalends of January, the Roman New Year, brought greenery and lamps on doorways and gifts called strenae, described by Libanius. Tertullian had already scolded Christians for hanging laurels and lamps at their doors on pagan festivals (De idololatria 15). Gregory of Nazianzus, preaching on the Nativity in Constantinople in 380, urged Christians not to garland their porches or feast like pagans but to celebrate 'in a heavenly manner'.

The church's response mixed condemnation with substitution. Sermons by Asterius of Amasea (c.400) and Caesarius of Arles (sixth century) attacked Kalends masquerades and gift-giving. The Council of Tours (567) made the twelve days from Christmas to Epiphany a festal season and also prescribed fasting at the Kalends to counter pagan revelry. Over time, feasting and gift-giving moved into the Christmas–Epiphany season, associated with the Magi's gifts and, later, with saints.

In northern Europe the Germanic midwinter supplied a name and a mood. Bede (De temporum ratione 15) records that the English called December and January Giuli. He says they began their year on 25 December with 'Modranecht', the 'night of the mothers'. In Norway, according to Snorri Sturluson's Heimskringla (c.1230), King Haakon the Good (d.961) ordered Yule to be kept at the same time as Christmas. Scandinavian languages still call Christmas jul, and English 'Yuletide' preserves the word. The details of pagan Yule rites are poorly attested, and Snorri wrote two and a half centuries later.

Many familiar customs are not ancient at all. The town accounts of Sélestat in Alsace (1521) and a Strasbourg description of 1605 record fir trees decorated with apples, wafers and paper roses. They were probably descended from the paradise tree of medieval mystery plays performed on 24 December, the feast of Adam and Eve. Lutheran Germany spread the custom, and Prince Albert and an 1848 engraving of the royal family made it fashionable in Britain. The Yule log is first recorded in seventeenth-century England (Robert Herrick). Kissing under mistletoe dates from the eighteenth century, though Pliny describes druids cutting mistletoe (Natural History 16.95).

Gift-bringers have a mainly Christian history. Nicholas, a fourth-century bishop of Myra whose relics were taken to Bari in 1087, became the patron of children through legends of secret dowries. Medieval Europe gave presents on his feast (6 December). Some Lutherans moved gift-giving to Christmas and the Christ-child (Christkind). Dutch Sinterklaas was reworked in New York by John Pintard, Washington Irving and the poem 'A Visit from St Nicholas' (1823), and Thomas Nast's drawings (from 1863) fixed the image of Santa Claus. Puritans banned Christmas revelry in the seventeenth century, partly as 'popish' and partly as heathen. Nineteenth-century writers such as Dickens then promoted a domestic Christmas that blended Christian, folk and commercial elements.
influences/christmas-customs/howItHappen: Fourth-century Christians carried Roman midwinter and New Year customs (greenery, lamps, gifts, feasting) into the new Nativity season.
Bishops condemned Kalends revelry while councils (Tours, 567) made the Twelve Days a Christian festal season.
In Anglo-Saxon England and Scandinavia the native midwinter name (Giuli, jól) attached itself to Christmas.
Medieval saints' cults, especially Nicholas (6 December), supplied gift-bringers.
Sixteenth- to nineteenth-century German, English and American developments added the tree, the Yule log, cards and Santa Claus.
influences/christmas-customs/examples/0: Gregory of Nazianzus, Oration 38 (380): do not crown your doorways or arrange dances.
influences/christmas-customs/examples/1: Council of Tours (567): the days between Christmas and Epiphany declared festal.
influences/christmas-customs/examples/2: Sélestat (1521) and Strasbourg (1605): earliest records of decorated Christmas trees.
influences/christmas-customs/examples/3: Scandinavian jul / English Yule: a pre-Christian name kept for Christmas.
influences/christmas-customs/examples/4: Saint Nicholas of Myra → Sinterklaas → Santa Claus ('A Visit from St Nicholas', 1823).
influences/christmas-customs/defenders/0: Associated in Lutheran lore with the lit Christmas tree and with moving gift-giving from Saint Nicholas to the Christ-child. The tree story itself is a nineteenth-century legend.
influences/christmas-customs/defenders/1: His 601 policy of letting converts keep feasting on Christian festivals (letter to Mellitus) was later cited as the model for absorbing Yule-tide celebration.
influences/christmas-customs/defenders/2: Recorded the English Giuli months and Modranecht without condemnation, showing native names carried into Christian time.
influences/christmas-customs/critics/0/t: Condemned Christians who decorated their doors with laurels and lamps during pagan festivals (De idololatria 15).
influences/christmas-customs/critics/1/t: Warned in 380 against garlands, dancing and feasting 'in the pagan manner' at the Nativity.
influences/christmas-customs/critics/2/t: Suppressed Christmas feasting, decorations and 'misrule' in England (1647) and New England as unscriptural and heathen.
influences/christmas-customs/keptBy/0: Most Western churches and Christian-heritage cultures
influences/christmas-customs/keptBy/1: Orthodox cultures, with their own customs such as the Slavic Sviatki and Saint Basil's day gifts in Greece
influences/christmas-customs/rejectedBy/: Some conservative Reformed, Restorationist and Hebrew Roots Christians who object to the tree (citing Jeremiah 10:3–4) and Santa Claus
influences/christmas-customs/calendar/ch: Christmas and the Twelve Days (25 December–6 January); Saint Nicholas on 6 December
influences/christmas-customs/calendar/pa: Saturnalia (17–23 December), Kalends of January, Germanic Yule / Modranecht
influences/christ-pantocrator-imperial/n: Christ Pantocrator, imperial ceremony and Byzantine art
influences/christ-pantocrator-imperial/s: Roman imperial portraiture and court ceremonial: the enthroned ruler, purple and gold, proskynesis, the adventus procession, and the enthroned Zeus/Jupiter type
influences/christ-pantocrator-imperial/c: Christ enthroned as heavenly emperor and Pantocrator (‘Ruler of all’), the Maiestas Domini, and courtly elements in liturgy and icon
influences/christ-pantocrator-imperial/e: That late Roman imperial art and ceremony shaped images of Christ enthroned and some elements of liturgy is widely accepted; how far is debated. André Grabar’s classic ‘imperial’ thesis has been challenged by Thomas Mathews, who argues that images of Christ drew more on pagan gods and philosophers than on emperors. The title Pantokrator itself is biblical, not pagan.
influences/christ-pantocrator-imperial/p: Once Constantine converted, the humble Jesus was turned into a Roman emperor and Christianity became an imperial religion modelled on the cult of Caesar.
influences/christ-pantocrator-imperial/w: Christian art after 313 did adopt forms from the court: Christ appears enthroned in gold and purple among apostles dressed as senators (Santa Pudenziana, c. 400), Palm Sunday scenes echo the imperial adventus, and gestures such as proskynesis passed into Byzantine devotion. But Pantokrator is the Septuagint’s translation of ‘Lord of hosts’ and ‘Almighty’ and appears in Revelation 1:8, so the idea of Christ as universal ruler predates any imperial influence. The bearded, enthroned Christ also echoes Phidias’s Zeus and images of philosophers, as Mathews stresses, and Christians often used imperial forms to relativise the emperor, who in mosaics bows before Christ. Scholars therefore speak of a two-way exchange in which court culture and the church borrowed from each other.
influences/christ-pantocrator-imperial/s: From the late fourth century Christ was increasingly shown as an enthroned, majestic ruler, drawing on Roman imperial and divine imagery; the biblical title Pantocrator was given visual form in the domes and icons of Byzantium.

Before Constantine, images of Christ were modest: a young shepherd, a teacher, a miracle-worker with a wand. After 313, and especially from the reign of Theodosius I (379–395), a new image appeared: Christ enthroned, bearded, robed in gold, surrounded by attendants. In the apse of Santa Pudenziana in Rome (c. 390–417) he sits on a jewelled throne with the heavenly Jerusalem behind him, and the apostles, in togas, resemble a senate. André Grabar’s L’Empereur dans l’art byzantin (1936) and his later Christian Iconography (1968) argued that such images were modelled directly on imperial art: the ruler enthroned in majesty, receiving homage, handing down the law.

Court ceremonial left marks on worship too. The emperor’s formal entry into a city (adventus), with crowds carrying branches, provided a template for depictions of Christ’s entry into Jerusalem. Proskynesis, the full prostration before the emperor adopted at court in the age of Diocletian, became a normal act of reverence before icons and the altar. Lights, incense and the carrying of the Gospel book in procession resembled honours paid to the emperor’s image and to magistrates. Sabine MacCormack’s Art and Ceremony in Late Antiquity traced how these rituals and their images moved between palace and church.

The Byzantine Pantocrator was the mature fruit of this development. The sixth-century encaustic icon at St Catherine’s Monastery, Sinai, shows Christ holding a jewelled Gospel book and blessing, his face subtly asymmetrical to suggest his two natures. After iconoclasm (726–843) the bust of the Pantocrator came to dominate the central domes of Byzantine churches, as at Daphni near Athens (c. 1100), and Norman Sicily imported the type into the apses of Cefalù (1148) and Monreale. In the Latin West the corresponding image was the Maiestas Domini, Christ enthroned within a mandorla among the four living creatures.

Yet the influence was not one-way, and its extent is disputed. Thomas Mathews, in The Clash of Gods (1993), argued that the ‘emperor mystique’ had been exaggerated: Christ’s long hair and beard echo Zeus and Asclepius, his miracles resemble the magician’s, and his teaching pose is that of the philosopher; early artists were competing with the pagan gods more than flattering the emperor. The word Pantokrator itself comes from the Greek Bible, where it renders ‘Lord of hosts’ (Sabaoth) and ‘Almighty’, and from Revelation 1:8. Imperial imagery could also be used to subordinate the emperor: in Hagia Sophia an emperor, probably Leo VI, prostrates himself before the enthroned Christ (late ninth or early tenth century).

The theological interpretation of this marriage has always divided Christians. Eusebius of Caesarea, in his oration for Constantine’s thirty years (336), saw the Christian empire as an image of the heavenly monarchy of the Logos, an outlook that shaped Byzantine political theology. Critics of the ‘Constantinian’ church, from medieval dissenters and Anabaptists to modern theologians, have argued that the imperial Christ obscured the crucified one. Historians generally conclude that the church took over the visual and ceremonial language of power available to it, while biblical and doctrinal content, especially the confession of Christ as fully divine at Nicaea (325) and Chalcedon (451), determined what that language was made to say.
influences/christ-pantocrator-imperial/h: After 313 Christian patrons, including emperors and aristocrats, commissioned church decoration from artists trained in imperial and civic art.
The Nicene confession of Christ as fully divine encouraged images that showed him as cosmic ruler rather than only as teacher or shepherd.
Court rituals of adventus, proskynesis and honour to the imperial image provided models for liturgical processions and veneration of icons.
Byzantine theology of the Christian empire, from Eusebius onwards, presented the emperor as earthly image of Christ’s heavenly rule.
After iconoclasm, the Pantocrator bust became the standard dome image of the Byzantine church interior.
influences/christ-pantocrator-imperial/e: Apse mosaic of Santa Pudenziana, Rome (c. 390–417): Christ enthroned among apostles in senatorial dress.
Encaustic icon of Christ Pantocrator, St Catherine’s Monastery, Sinai (sixth century).
Apse of San Vitale, Ravenna (547): a youthful Christ seated on the globe, offering a crown to St Vitalis.
Narthex mosaic of an emperor (probably Leo VI) prostrate before Christ, Hagia Sophia, Constantinople (c. 886–912).
Dome Pantocrator at Daphni monastery, near Athens (c. 1100), and apse Pantocrator at Cefalù cathedral, Sicily (1148).
influences/christ-pantocrator-imperial/d: In his Tricennial Oration (336) and Life of Constantine presented the Christian emperor as image of the Logos’s heavenly monarchy, the foundation of Byzantine political theology.
Used the analogy of honour paid to the emperor’s image to explain why veneration of an icon passes to Christ himself (On the Divine Images).
influences/christ-pantocrator-imperial/c: The iconoclast emperor argued in his Peuseis (c. 750s) that Christ, being divine, could not be truly portrayed, and attacked the cult of images.
Art historian whose The Clash of Gods (1993) argued against the ‘imperial’ interpretation, tracing images of Christ to pagan gods, magicians and philosophers instead.
influences/christ-pantocrator-imperial/k: Eastern Orthodox churches, where the Pantocrator in the dome and on the iconostasis is central to the church’s visual theology.
Eastern Catholic churches of the Byzantine rite.
Catholic and Anglican art in the form of Christ in Majesty, Christ the King (feast instituted 1925).
influences/christ-pantocrator-imperial/r: Byzantine iconoclasts (726–787, 815–843), who rejected images of Christ.
Reformed and other Protestant traditions that exclude images of Christ from worship.
Anabaptist and other critics of ‘Constantinian’ Christianity, who reject the imperial model of Christ and church.
